conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. You were brought in from rehab because of vomiting—can you tell me about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had two episodes this morning. The rehab staff got worried because it looked dark, almost like coffee grounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had gastroparesis for a while—has vomiting like this happened before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do vomit sometimes. It’s usually brownish. I didn’t feel any different this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You’re not having abdominal pain, nausea, or shortness of breath now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel okay now. Just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your blood—your hemoglobin is stable at 7.7, which is your usual level. That’s reassuring. We also did a stool test, and it was negative for blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. The GI team thinks the dark color could be from irritation in your esophagus, maybe from your feeding tube. We don’t think you need an endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had that tube for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring you. We also noticed your troponin was slightly elevated. Did you have any chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your EKG doesn’t show any signs of a heart attack. The troponin is probably elevated because of your kidney issues, not a new heart problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on dialysis, so that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll continue your regular dialysis. You’re scheduled for it tomorrow at noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also reviewed your chest X-ray. It shows some fluid in your lungs, which we’ve seen before. No pneumonia or new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that since my surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s chronic. We’ll manage it with dialysis and your heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs overnight were stable. No further vomiting, and your kidney function is consistent with baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t vomited again. I did feel a little nauseous earlier, but it passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on Zofran for nausea, as needed. It might help prevent vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’ve taken it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked a stool test for C. difficile, which came back negative. So no infection there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit tired, but okay. No nausea so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is stable. We’ll keep an eye on your volume status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your medications. You’re now on metoprolol, which helps your heart after bypass surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I wasn’t on that before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, but it’s standard after CABG. It protects your heart and helps with blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re planning to discharge you back to rehab today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That was fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ve been stable, no more vomiting, and your labs haven’t changed. The team feels you’re safe to return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the warfarin? I remember my INR was high last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We held one dose because your INR was 3.2, but you’ll restart at your usual 3 mg daily. Cardiology will follow up on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Zofran?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take it as needed for nausea—4 mg every 8 hours if needed. Keep an eye on the vomiting and let rehab know if it happens again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send all the details to your rehab team. Take care.
